notes.meaning: The queen of Sheba, a rich land in southern Arabia, heard about Solomon's fame and his devotion to the LORD. She traveled to Jerusalem to test his famous wisdom with hard riddles and questions. She wanted to see for herself whether the amazing reports were true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars consider the queen historically unlikely because ancient surviving lists of Sabaean leaders mention only male rulers.

notes.meaning: The queen arrived in Jerusalem with a very large caravan of camels carrying sweet spices, piles of gold, and precious gems. When she met Solomon, she spoke openly with him about everything on her mind. Her rich gifts showed both the wealth of her kingdom and the high honor she gave the king.
Solomon answered every single question the queen asked. Nothing was too hard, confusing, or hidden for him to explain. God had given him the wisdom to solve every puzzle she brought before him.

The queen saw Solomon's great wisdom at work everywhere in his court. She was amazed by his palace, the food on his tables, the seating of his officials, the uniforms of his servants, and the burnt offerings he presented at the temple. The sheer beauty and order of it all took her breath away.

The queen told Solomon that the glowing reports she had heard back home were completely true. She admitted that she had not believed the stories until she came and saw everything with her own eyes. The truth far exceeded the rumors, for not even half the story had been told to her.

The queen called Solomon's people and his servants truly blessed. His court attendants had the special privilege of standing near him every day to hear his wise words. Being near godly wisdom is a far greater treasure than any earthly riches.

The queen praised the LORD, the God of Israel, for placing Solomon on the throne. She recognized that God made him king because of His lasting love for Israel, choosing him to lead with fairness and justice. A godly ruler is given by God to protect and serve the people.

The queen gave Solomon about four and a half tons of gold, along with precious stones and a huge quantity of spices. Israel had never seen such an abundance of fine spices as the gift she presented. Her generous presents sealed an alliance of friendship and deep mutual respect.

King Hiram's trading ships also brought back vast amounts of gold, gems, and rare almug wood from Ophir. Solomon used this prized timber to make stair railings for the temple and palace, as well as lyres and harps for the musicians. Such fine, beautiful wood had never been seen in Israel before or since.

Solomon granted the queen of Sheba everything she asked for, on top of rich gifts given out of his own royal bounty. After their visit ended, she and her servants packed up and returned home to Arabia. Their peaceful meeting showed how rulers can treat one another with honor and generosity.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: An old Ethiopian tradition teaches that the queen had a son with Solomon named Menelik, who became king and took the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia.

notes.meaning: Solomon received about twenty-five tons of gold into his royal treasury each year. This enormous sum did not even include extra income from trade duties, traveling merchants, Arabian kings, and local governors. Israel had become the wealthy center of major international trade routes.

differ.view: Some evangelicals see a link between this 666 and the number of the beast. They suggest the Antichrist may be like Solomon, a gifted man spoiled by power and wealth.

notes.meaning: Solomon crafted two hundred large shields and three hundred smaller shields out of beaten gold. These golden shields were placed in the House of the Forest of Lebanon to be displayed during royal ceremonies rather than used in actual combat. They stood as visible symbols of the wealth and glory of his reign.

Solomon built a magnificent throne inlaid with precious ivory and coated with fine gold. The mix of gleaming white ivory and pure gold gave it an unmatched, stunning appearance. It was the central seat where the king sat to give wise and fair decisions.

The throne had six steps leading up to it, a rounded back, armrests, and two carved lions standing beside the seat. Twelve more lions stood along the six steps, with one at each end of every step. No other royal throne in any ancient kingdom compared to its beauty and power.

All of Solomon's drinking cups and the utensils in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were made of pure gold. No silver was used for these royal items because it was considered ordinary and of little value during his reign. God gave Solomon such plenty that precious metals filled the court.

Solomon kept a fleet of large trading ships at sea alongside Hiram's Phoenician sailors. Every three years the ships returned to port loaded with gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks. These exotic items showed just how far Solomon's reach stretched across the ancient world.

Solomon surpassed all the kings on earth in both riches and wisdom. God fully kept His promise to bless Solomon with honor alongside the understanding he had asked for. His kingdom reached the very height of its worldly splendor.

Rulers and visitors from all nations sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. Year after year, every visitor brought gifts of silver and gold items, fine clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules. People gladly honored him because of the help and counsel they received from his teaching.

Solomon gathered a huge military force of 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses. He stationed them in specially built chariot cities throughout the land and kept part of the force with him in Jerusalem. This gave Israel a strong national defense during a time of general peace.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe Solomon was wrong to build up so many horses, pointing out that God specifically commanded Israel's kings in Deuteronomy 17:16 not to multiply horses or rely on military power.

notes.meaning: Solomon made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones on the ground. Precious cedar wood became as plentiful as the wild sycamore-fig trees that grew in the foothills. This picture emphasizes the incredible prosperity God poured out upon the capital city during these golden years.

Solomon's merchants imported fine horses and chariots from Egypt and Cilicia at set market prices. The king then served as an international middleman, selling these horses and chariots to the kings of Syria and the Hittites. This trade made Israel the major commercial crossroad for military supplies in the region.
